hero.eyebrow: Spreadsheet skills · No software to install
hero.title: Basic Microsoft Excel: learn by doing
hero.subtitle: Type data, write formulas, make decisions with IF, sort, filter and chart, in a working spreadsheet inside your browser. Every step is checked and explained.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can build a clean, working spreadsheet from scratch and present it with a chart.

outcomes.title: Write formulas

outcomes.title: Summarise with functions
outcomes.text: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT and ROUND.

outcomes.title: Make decisions
outcomes.text: IF, AND, OR, COUNTIF and SUMIF to answer real questions.

outcomes.title: Organise data

outcomes.title: Chart and report

assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the final project and the final assessment to finish the course.

faq.q: Do I need Microsoft Excel installed?
faq.a: No. The labs run in your browser with a spreadsheet that behaves like Excel for everything taught here. The skills carry straight over to Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice.
About seven hours, in short sessions. Each module takes around an hour.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your GrowQR profile.

activities.title: Type a price list
activities.objective: Enter text and numbers in the right cells and make the heading row stand out.
activities.scenario: A stationery shop wants a price list: the item in column A, the price in column B and the stock in column C.
steps: Click A2 and type four items, one per row (for example Pen, Notebook, Eraser, Ruler).
Type a price for each item in B2:B5 and a stock count in C2:C5.
Make the headings in row 1 bold, then format the prices as currency.

checks.label: Four items in A2:A5
checks.hint: Click A2, type a name and press Enter to move down.
checks.explain: Each row is one product, so each product gets its own row.

checks.label: Prices and stock in B2:C5
checks.hint: Type plain numbers, such as 12 or 250, without any words.
checks.explain: Numbers must be typed as numbers (not as text) so formulas can use them later.

checks.label: Heading A1 is bold
checks.hint: Click A1 and press the bold button B in the toolbar.
checks.explain: Bold headings tell the reader which cells are labels and which are data.

checks.label: Price B2 is formatted as currency
checks.hint: Click B2, then choose Currency in the Number format list.
checks.explain: A number format changes how a value looks, never the value itself.

activities.title: Build an invoice
activities.objective: Write formulas that use cell references instead of typed numbers.
activities.scenario: Asha sold three items. Work out the amount for each line (quantity times price) and the invoice total.
steps: In D2 type a formula that multiplies the quantity in B2 by the price in C2.
Do the same for D3 and D4 with their own rows.
In D5 add the three amounts together with a formula.

checks.label: D2 multiplies B2 by C2
checks.hint: Type =B2*C2 and press Enter. Start with the equals sign.
checks.explain: A formula that points at cells updates by itself if the quantity or price changes.

checks.label: D3 is the amount for Pen
checks.hint: Use the same idea with row 3: B3 times C3.
checks.explain: Each row needs its own cell references.

checks.label: D4 is the amount for Folder
checks.hint: Multiply B4 by C4.
checks.explain: Check the answer by doing 3 times 30 in your head.

checks.label: D5 adds the three amounts
checks.hint: Try =SUM(D2:D4).
checks.explain: SUM adds every number in a range, so you do not type each cell.

activities.title: Add tax with an absolute reference
activities.objective: Keep one cell fixed with a dollar sign while the rest of the formula changes row by row.
activities.scenario: The tax rate sits in one cell (B1). Every price must use that same cell, so changing the rate once updates the whole sheet.
steps: In C4 type a formula for the tax on the price in B4: the price times the rate in B1. Lock the rate with dollar signs ($B$1).
In C5 and C6 do the same for their own prices; the rate cell must stay B1.
In D4 add the price and its tax; copy the idea to D5 and D6.

checks.label: C4 uses the price in B4 and the locked rate $B$1
checks.hint: Type =B4*$B$1. The dollar signs lock column B and row 1.
checks.explain: Without dollar signs the rate reference would slide down to B2, B3 and break.

checks.label: C5 gives the tax for the bottle
checks.hint: Use B5 for the price, but keep $B$1 for the rate.
checks.explain: The price reference changes by row; the rate reference must not.

checks.label: C6 gives the tax for the lunch box
checks.hint: Same pattern: =B6*$B$1.
checks.explain: A locked reference is called an absolute reference.

checks.label: D6 is price plus tax for the lunch box
checks.hint: Try =B6+C6.
checks.explain: Total price is the price plus the tax on it.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: If a cell shows #VALUE!, check that B1 holds a number or a percentage.
checks.explain: Errors mean a formula cannot be worked out.

activities.title: Summarise a class's marks
activities.objective: Use SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN and COUNT on a range.
activities.scenario: A teacher has maths marks for six students and wants the key numbers at the bottom of the sheet.
steps: In B9 total the marks with SUM.
In B10 find the average with AVERAGE.
In B11 and B12 find the highest and lowest marks.
In B13 count how many marks have been entered.

checks.label: B9 totals the marks
checks.hint: =SUM(B2:B7)
checks.explain: SUM adds numbers in the range you give it.

checks.label: B10 is the average
checks.hint: =AVERAGE(B2:B7)
checks.explain: The average is the total divided by how many numbers there are, which AVERAGE does for you.

checks.label: B11 is the highest mark
checks.hint: =MAX(B2:B7)
checks.explain: MAX looks through the range and gives back the biggest number.

checks.label: B12 is the lowest mark
checks.hint: =MIN(B2:B7)
checks.explain: MIN gives the smallest number in the range.

checks.label: B13 counts the marks
checks.hint: =COUNT(B2:B7)
checks.explain: COUNT counts cells that hold numbers.

activities.title: Pass or fail with IF
activities.objective: Make a cell decide between two answers with IF.
activities.scenario: A mark of 40 or more is a pass. Show Pass or Fail next to each mark, then count how many students passed.
steps: In C2 write an IF that shows Pass when B2 is 40 or more and Fail otherwise.
Write the same kind of formula in C3 to C6 for their own rows.
In B8 count how many students passed with COUNTIF on column C.

checks.label: C2 shows Pass for Gita
checks.hint: =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Fail")
checks.explain: IF has three parts: a test, the answer if true, the answer if false.

checks.label: C3 shows Fail for Harsh
checks.hint: Same formula, but with B3.
checks.explain: 38 is below 40, so the test is false.

checks.label: C4 shows Pass for Imran (exactly 40)
checks.hint: Use >= (greater than or equal), not just >.
checks.explain: Exactly 40 passes. The sign you choose decides what happens at the boundary.

checks.label: C6 shows Pass for Kabir
checks.hint: Fill the last row too.
checks.explain: Every row needs its own IF with its own marks cell.

checks.label: B8 counts the passes
checks.hint: =COUNTIF(C2:C6,"Pass")
checks.explain: COUNTIF counts the cells in a range that match a condition.

activities.title: Sales by region
activities.objective: Add up only the rows that match a condition with SUMIF, and count them with COUNTIF.
activities.scenario: A small business sells in three regions. The owner wants the total for each region and how many orders each had.
steps: In F2 total the amounts for the North region with SUMIF (look in column A for "North", add column B).
In F3 and F4 do the same for South and East.
In G2 count the North orders with COUNTIF.

checks.label: F2 gives the North total
checks.hint: =SUMIF(A2:A8,E2,B2:B8)
checks.explain: SUMIF adds the amounts only where the region matches.

checks.label: F3 gives the South total
checks.hint: Use E3 as the condition.
checks.explain: Pointing at E3 means the formula follows the label in that row.

checks.label: F4 gives the East total
checks.hint: Use E4 as the condition.
checks.explain: Three regions, three SUMIF formulas.

checks.label: G2 counts North orders
checks.hint: =COUNTIF(A2:A8,E2)
checks.explain: COUNTIF counts the rows that match, whatever their amount.

activities.title: Sort a list from highest to lowest
activities.objective: Sort a table by one column without breaking its rows.
activities.scenario: A coach has recorded 100 metre times in seconds and wants the fastest runners first.
steps: Select the whole table, A1 to B7.
Use the Sort tool on column B and choose smallest to largest.
Check that every name still sits next to its own time.

checks.label: Times are sorted smallest to largest
checks.hint: Select A1:B7, choose column B and smallest to largest.
checks.explain: Fastest means the smallest time, so ascending order puts them first.

checks.label: No row was lost
checks.hint: Sort the whole table, including the names column.
checks.explain: Sorting only one column would separate names from times.

checks.label: Priya, the fastest, is first
checks.hint: After a correct sort the first name is Priya.
checks.explain: A sorted table keeps each name with its own time.

activities.title: Turn numbers into a chart
activities.objective: Choose the right chart type and build it from a table.
activities.scenario: A shop wants to see which month sold the most. A column chart compares separate months best.
steps: Check that the months are in A2:A5 and the sales in B2:B5.
Add a bar (column) chart using A2:A5 as labels and B2:B5 as values.
Give the chart a title that says what it shows.

checks.label: A bar chart uses A2:A5 and B2:B5
checks.hint: Select the table, choose Bar as the chart type, and add the chart.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares amounts across separate categories such as months.

checks.label: Sales are filled in B2:B5
checks.hint: Do not delete the data the chart is built from.
checks.explain: A chart is only as good as its data.

activities.title: Which function does the job?
activities.objective: Match a task to the function that does it.
activities.scenario: You know the five basic functions. Now choose the right one for each task.
steps: Read each task.
Choose the function that does it.
Press Check my work.

steps: Read the situation.
Pick the error it would produce.
Press Check my work.

activities.title: Monthly shop report
activities.objective: Combine formulas, IF, SUMIF, an absolute reference and a chart in one working report.
activities.scenario: A shop owner gives you a week of sales. Prepare the report: totals, a target check, a category summary and a chart.
steps: In D2:D7 work out each line's amount (units times price).
In D8 total the amounts.
In E2:E7 show Met or Missed: Met when the amount reaches the target in B10 (lock it with $B$10).
In G2 and G3 use SUMIF to total the Snacks and Drinks categories.
Add a bar chart of the category totals F2:F3 against G2:G3.

checks.label: Line amounts are formulas (D2 to D7)
checks.hint: In D2 type =B2*C2 and write the same idea in each row.
checks.explain: Formulas keep the report correct when units or prices change.

checks.label: The last line, Water, is correct
checks.hint: Row 7: units 50 times price 15.
checks.explain: Check the final row too: it is the one most often forgotten.

checks.label: D8 is the total of all amounts
checks.hint: =SUM(D2:D7)
checks.explain: The total of the six lines.

checks.label: E2 shows Missed for Chips (400 is below 500)
checks.hint: =IF(D2>=$B$10,"Met","Missed")
checks.explain: The target is locked with dollar signs so every row compares to the same cell.

checks.label: E7 shows Met for Water (750 is above 500)
checks.hint: Use the same formula in E7.
checks.explain: The same locked target works down the whole column.

checks.label: G2 totals Snacks
checks.hint: =SUMIF(H2:H7,F2,D2:D7)
checks.explain: SUMIF adds only the rows where the category matches.

checks.label: G3 totals Drinks
checks.hint: Use F3 as the condition.
checks.explain: Snacks plus drinks should equal the grand total.

checks.label: A bar chart of the categories
checks.hint: Chart type Bar, labels F2:F3, values G2:G3.
checks.explain: A bar chart compares the two categories at a glance.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: Click any cell showing an error and read its message.
checks.explain: A report with errors cannot be trusted.
